options.a: Flexibility and muscular strength first, then cardio and resting measures
options.b: Resting measures, body composition, cardio, muscular fitness, flexibility
options.c: Muscular strength first, then resting HR and BP, then the cardio test
options.d: Cardiorespiratory test first, then body composition and resting BP

distractorExplanations.a: Resting HR and BP must be taken before exercise raises them, so they come first, not last.
distractorExplanations.c: Strength testing first raises HR and BP and fatigues the client before the cardio test.
distractorExplanations.d: A cardio test first raises HR and BP and can distort body-composition readings such as BIA.

options.a: Static plumb-line posture check
options.b: Sit-and-reach flexibility test
options.c: Resting blood pressure
options.d: Overhead squat assessment

distractorExplanations.a: A plumb-line check views static standing posture; it does not load the kinetic chain through movement like the OHSA.
distractorExplanations.b: Sit-and-reach measures hamstring and low-back flexibility at one range, not movement compensations under load.
distractorExplanations.c: BP is a vital sign, not a movement screen.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-003.explanation: The overhead squat assessment observes dynamic movement compensations along the kinetic chain; a plumb-line check is static, and sit-and-reach and BP give other data types.

options.a: Weak hip abductors and external rotators, such as gluteus medius
options.b: Weak ankle plantar flexors, such as the soleus and gastrocnemius
options.c: Tight hamstrings pulling the pelvis into a posterior tilt
options.d: Weak quadriceps that cannot extend the knee under load

distractorExplanations.b: Weak plantar flexors do not pull the knees inward; valgus is a frontal-plane hip control problem.
distractorExplanations.c: Posterior pelvic tilt from tight hamstrings shows as a rounded low back, not knees caving in.
distractorExplanations.d: Quadriceps weakness limits depth or knee extension, but does not by itself drive the knees medially.

options.a: Estimate VO2max so a submaximal treadmill test can be skipped
options.b: Screen for health risks and flag need for medical clearance
options.c: Replace the informed consent form before training begins
options.d: Classify the client's fitness level for program design

distractorExplanations.a: The PAR-Q+ is a health-history questionnaire; it cannot estimate aerobic capacity or substitute for a fitness test.
distractorExplanations.c: Screening and informed consent are separate documents; one does not replace the other.
distractorExplanations.d: Fitness level comes from assessments, not from a health-risk questionnaire.

options.a: Reduce the load and continue if the pain eases
options.b: Switch to the same movement on a machine
options.c: Apply ice and resume after a short rest break
options.d: Stop the movement and refer for medical review

distractorExplanations.a: Sharp joint pain is a stop signal, not something to train around with lighter load.
distractorExplanations.b: Changing equipment still loads the painful joint without knowing the cause.
distractorExplanations.c: Resuming after ice ignores a red-flag symptom that needs evaluation.

options.a: Whether the client already exercises regularly
options.b: The client's resting blood pressure category
options.c: The number of CVD risk factors the client reports
options.d: The client's age and body mass index category

distractorExplanations.c: Counting CVD risk factors was the pre-2015 approach; the current algorithm dropped risk-factor tallies.
distractorExplanations.b: BP is useful data, but the current algorithm does not start from BP category.
distractorExplanations.d: Age and BMI are not decision points in the current preparticipation algorithm.

options.a: Tight calves or hip flexors with a weak posterior chain
options.b: Tight hamstrings with weak hip flexors and quadriceps
options.c: Weak calves with overactive tibialis anterior muscles
options.d: Tight latissimus dorsi with weak lower-trapezius muscles

distractorExplanations.d: Tight lats with weak middle and lower traps produce the arms-fall-forward compensation, not excessive trunk lean.
distractorExplanations.b: Tight hamstrings pull the pelvis back; they do not cause excessive forward lean.
distractorExplanations.c: Weak calves and an overactive tibialis would ease dorsiflexion, not limit it.

options.a: Frequency, intensity, time, type, volume, and progression
options.b: Frequency, intensity, tempo, type, variety, and progression
options.c: Frequency, interval, training load, type, velocity, pace
options.d: Fitness, intensity, time, technique, volume, and posture

distractorExplanations.b: Tempo and variety are not FITT-VP letters; the second T stands for time (duration) and the V for volume.
distractorExplanations.c: Interval, training load, velocity, and pace are not part of FITT-VP.
distractorExplanations.d: Fitness, technique, and posture are not the FITT-VP components.

options.a: A week of 1RM testing to set new training loads
options.b: A planned drop in volume or intensity for recovery
options.c: A week off all exercise after an injury diagnosis
options.d: A planned week of extra volume to push past a plateau

distractorExplanations.d: Planned extra volume is a functional overreaching block, the opposite of a deload's reduced training load.
distractorExplanations.a: Maximal testing adds stress; a deload reduces it.
distractorExplanations.c: A deload keeps some training; it is not injury rest.

options.a: 2–3 days a week, 8–10 exercises, starting at 1 set of 8–12
options.b: 5–6 days a week, 3 exercises, 5 sets of 3 reps at 90% 1RM
options.c: 1 day a week, 20 exercises, 3 sets to failure for each one
options.d: Daily sessions, 2 exercises, 10 sets of 15 reps each

distractorExplanations.b: Low-rep, high-set work is a strength block for trained lifters, not a novice start.
distractorExplanations.c: Once a week is too infrequent, and 20 exercises to failure is excessive for a novice.
distractorExplanations.d: Daily training of the same muscles leaves no recovery for a beginner.

options.a: Maximal strength through low-rep heavy lifting
options.b: Aerobic capacity through long steady-state work
options.c: Acceleration, change of direction, and reaction
options.d: Muscle hypertrophy through moderate-rep sets

distractorExplanations.a: Heavy low-rep work builds maximal strength, not agility.
distractorExplanations.b: Long steady work builds aerobic capacity.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypertrophy comes from resistance volume, not agility drills.

options.a: Lengthen muscles with long static stretches
options.b: Raise tissue temperature and rehearse movements
options.c: Pre-fatigue the target muscles before the heavy sets
options.d: Lower heart rate before the working sets begin

distractorExplanations.c: Pre-fatiguing target muscles lowers force in the working sets; it is an advanced intensity technique, not a warm-up goal.
distractorExplanations.a: Long static holds before lifting can briefly reduce force output.
distractorExplanations.d: A warm-up raises heart rate gradually; it does not lower it.

options.a: Muscles that only produce movement in the sagittal plane
options.b: Muscles that work together to stabilize and move a joint
options.c: Muscles that oppose the prime mover during an action
options.d: Muscles that attach to the same bone at both ends

distractorExplanations.a: Synergists can act in any plane; plane is not what defines them.
distractorExplanations.c: Muscles that oppose the prime mover are antagonists.
distractorExplanations.d: A muscle attaching to one bone at both ends could not move a joint.

options.a: Muscular endurance: high reps, low load, short rest
options.b: Maximal strength: low reps, heavy load, long rest
options.c: Power: explosive reps with light-to-moderate loads and full rest
options.d: Hypertrophy: moderate reps and moderate rest

distractorExplanations.c: Power training needs an established strength and technique base, so it comes well after the initial endurance phase.
distractorExplanations.b: Heavy low-rep work is a later phase once technique and tolerance are built.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypertrophy work usually follows an initial endurance and technique phase.

options.a: Myofibril
options.b: Sarcomere
options.c: Fascicle
options.d: Sarcolemma

distractorExplanations.a: A myofibril is the rod of repeating sarcomeres inside the fiber; the sarcomere is the smallest contractile unit within it.
distractorExplanations.c: A fascicle is a bundle of whole muscle fibers wrapped in perimysium, a level above the fiber, not a unit inside it.
distractorExplanations.d: The sarcolemma is the fiber's cell membrane that conducts the action potential; it does not generate force itself.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-science-008.explanation: Sarcomeres (actin/myosin arrangement between Z-lines) are the smallest contractile units; myofibrils are chains of sarcomeres, fascicles bundle whole fibers, and the sarcolemma is the cell membrane.

options.a: Heavy squats and jump squats done on separate training days
options.b: A light plyometric drill followed by a 1RM test
options.c: A heavy lift paired with a similar explosive move
options.d: Isometric holds followed by long steady cardio

distractorExplanations.a: Splitting the heavy and explosive lifts across days removes the post-activation potentiation that defines complex training.
distractorExplanations.b: A 1RM test is a test, not a contrast training pair.
distractorExplanations.d: Isometrics and steady cardio do not train power.

options.a: Stabilize the lumbar spine by raising intra-abdominal pressure
options.b: Flex the trunk as the prime mover during sit-ups and crunches
options.c: Rotate the trunk as the prime mover during cable woodchops
options.d: Extend the lumbar spine as the prime mover during back extensions

distractorExplanations.d: Lumbar extension is driven by the erector spinae, a global mover, not by the deep transverse abdominis stabilizer.
distractorExplanations.b: The rectus abdominis is the prime mover for trunk flexion.
distractorExplanations.c: The obliques are the prime movers for trunk rotation.

options.a: It is fully shortened with sarcomeres overlapping
options.b: It is stretched to the end of its range of motion
options.c: Actin and myosin overlap optimally near rest length
options.d: It is contracting concentrically at its fastest velocity

distractorExplanations.d: That describes the force-velocity relationship: force falls as concentric speed rises, so maximal velocity gives low force.
distractorExplanations.a: When fully shortened, filaments overlap too much and force drops.
distractorExplanations.b: When overstretched, too few cross-bridges can form.

options.a: Is the primary mover producing the desired joint action
options.b: Relaxes to allow the desired joint action to happen
options.c: Assists the prime mover in producing the same joint action
options.d: Holds nearby joints steady while the movement happens

distractorExplanations.c: A muscle that assists the prime mover with the same action is a synergist, not the agonist itself.
distractorExplanations.b: The antagonist relaxes and lengthens to allow the action.
distractorExplanations.d: Muscles that hold nearby joints steady are stabilizers.

options.a: Collaborative exploration of ambivalence and motivation
options.b: Direct advice on the fastest way to reach client goals
options.c: Clear consequences when the client misses sessions
options.d: Detailed education on the health risks of staying inactive

distractorExplanations.d: Risk education can support change, but MI centers on evoking the client's own reasons rather than lecturing on risks.
distractorExplanations.b: MI evokes the client's own reasons rather than leading with advice.
distractorExplanations.c: Consequences and pressure increase resistance; MI avoids them.

options.a: Increasing sweat rate so the body cools more efficiently
options.b: Reducing plasma volume and raising cardiovascular strain
options.c: Lowering heart rate at a given workload during exercise
options.d: Increasing blood volume available to the working muscles

distractorExplanations.a: Dehydration reduces sweating capacity and raises core temperature.
distractorExplanations.c: Heart rate rises at a given workload when plasma volume falls (cardiovascular drift).
distractorExplanations.d: Fluid loss lowers blood volume; it does not increase it.

options.a: Build a low-carbohydrate meal plan and review glucose logs
options.b: Suggest a calorie target and remind the client to test
options.c: Provide sample diabetic menus from a trusted website
options.d: Refer to a dietitian or physician for nutrition therapy

distractorExplanations.a: Designing a disease-specific meal plan and reviewing glucose logs is medical nutrition therapy, outside CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.b: Setting targets for a diabetic client is clinical nutrition therapy.
distractorExplanations.c: Handing out diabetic menus is still individualized medical nutrition advice.

options.a: Prioritize sleep, planned progression, and nutrition
options.b: Use daily ice baths after every training session
options.c: Take a full week off training after every 2 weeks
options.d: Stretch statically for 20 minutes after each session

distractorExplanations.b: Frequent cold water immersion can blunt strength and hypertrophy gains.
distractorExplanations.c: This is far more rest than typical periodization requires.
distractorExplanations.d: Static stretching has little effect on recovery or soreness.

options.a: Moderate intake improves muscle protein synthesis
options.b: Alcohol calories are not stored as body fat
options.c: Excess intake can impair recovery, sleep, and diet
options.d: Alcohol rehydrates well after an endurance session

distractorExplanations.a: Alcohol reduces muscle protein synthesis after training.
distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol provides 7 kcal/g, and those calories can contribute to fat gain.
distractorExplanations.d: Alcohol is a diuretic and can worsen post-exercise dehydration.

options.a: Recommend brands that carry third-party testing seals
options.b: Share general evidence and refer clinical questions
options.c: Sell supplements only if the client asks for them
options.d: Suggest doses based on the client's body weight

distractorExplanations.a: Third-party seals reduce contamination risk, but recommending specific products still stretches CPT scope of practice.
distractorExplanations.c: Selling products creates a conflict of interest and is not evidence-based guidance.
distractorExplanations.d: Individual dosing is clinical advice outside CPT scope.

options.a: Simple, Motivating, Achievable, Rewarding, Tracked
options.b: Specific, Meaningful, Active, Reviewed, Targeted
options.c: Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, Time-bound
options.d: Strategic, Measured, Agreed, Realistic, Timed

distractorExplanations.a: These words are not the standard SMART acronym.
distractorExplanations.b: Meaningful, Active, Reviewed, and Targeted are not SMART terms.
distractorExplanations.d: Strategic and Agreed are not in the standard acronym.

options.a: Reduces short-term rises from activity, caffeine, or stress
options.b: Lets the cuff warm to body temperature for a steady reading
options.c: Is the time an automatic monitor needs to calibrate itself
options.d: Allows blood to pool in the legs for a lower reading

distractorExplanations.b: Cuff temperature does not affect the reading.
distractorExplanations.c: Monitors do not need a calibration period between clients.
distractorExplanations.d: The goal is a stable resting value, not an artificially low one.

options.a: The trainer's certifications and their expiry dates
options.b: That the waiver removes liability for all injuries
options.c: Activities, risks, and the right to stop at any time
options.d: The expected results and a timeline to reach them

distractorExplanations.a: Credentials may be shared, but they are not the core of informed consent.
distractorExplanations.b: Consent documents do not remove liability for negligence.
distractorExplanations.d: Promising results is not part of consent and can mislead the client.

options.a: Upper-body muscular endurance
options.b: Maximal lower-body power
options.c: Static hamstring flexibility
options.d: Resting metabolic rate

distractorExplanations.b: Power requires speed-loaded measures.
distractorExplanations.c: Hamstrings are not the primary push-up limiter.
distractorExplanations.d: RMR is not measured by push-ups.

options.a: Take one reading per site to avoid compressing tissue
options.b: Average readings that fall within the protocol's range
options.c: Use the highest reading at each site for safety
options.d: Measure on the left side of the body for accuracy

distractorExplanations.a: A single reading is unreliable; protocols require repeat measurements.
distractorExplanations.c: Choosing the highest value biases the estimate upward.
distractorExplanations.d: Most US protocols, including ACSM's, use the right side of the body.

options.a: Can talk in full sentences but cannot sing
options.b: Can sing comfortably while keeping pace
options.c: Can speak only a few words between breaths
options.d: Cannot speak without stopping to catch breath

distractorExplanations.d: Being unable to speak without pausing for breath signals near-maximal effort, well above moderate intensity.
distractorExplanations.b: Being able to sing suggests light intensity.
distractorExplanations.c: Only a few words at a time suggests vigorous intensity.

options.a: A 45-year-old with controlled hypertension on medication
options.b: A 60-year-old walker with a knee replacement last year
options.c: A 52-year-old with uncontrolled hypertension and syncope
options.d: A 38-year-old with type 1 diabetes and good control

distractorExplanations.a: Controlled hypertension usually allows training with monitoring.
distractorExplanations.b: A healed joint replacement may limit impact but is not a cardiac red flag.
distractorExplanations.d: Well-controlled diabetes needs glucose monitoring, not deferral of all testing.

options.a: Resting HR, maximal HR, and the target intensity
options.b: Resting HR, age, and the client's body weight
options.c: Maximal HR, blood pressure, and target intensity
options.d: Resting BP, age, and the client's RPE rating

distractorExplanations.b: Body weight is not part of the HRR formula.
distractorExplanations.c: Blood pressure is not used in the Karvonen formula.
distractorExplanations.d: The formula uses heart rates, not BP or RPE.

options.a: 150 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity
options.b: 75 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity
options.c: 300 minutes a week of vigorous aerobic activity
options.d: 30 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity

distractorExplanations.b: 75 minutes is the vigorous-intensity equivalent, not the moderate target.
distractorExplanations.c: 300 minutes is the upper moderate range for added benefit, not the vigorous minimum.
distractorExplanations.d: 30 minutes a week is far below the recommended minimum.

options.a: Lowering reps and raising load, with longer rest
options.b: Raising reps and lowering load, with less rest
options.c: Keeping reps the same and adding more sets
options.d: Switching to explosive reps with light loads

distractorExplanations.b: Higher reps with lighter loads shift toward endurance.
distractorExplanations.c: More sets at the same reps adds volume, not a strength emphasis.
distractorExplanations.d: Explosive light loads train power, which usually follows a strength phase.

options.a: A heavy upper-body session to rest the legs
options.b: Complete rest with no movement for two days
options.c: Light walking or mobility work at low effort
options.d: Moderate squats to flush out the soreness

distractorExplanations.a: A heavy session is not recovery, even for different muscles.
distractorExplanations.b: Complete inactivity is not needed after a normal hard session.
distractorExplanations.d: More squatting adds stress to the same tired muscles.

options.a: Lower heart rate allowing longer filling time
options.b: Greater venous return and stronger contraction
options.c: Reduced blood volume from sweating
options.d: Increased peripheral vascular resistance

distractorExplanations.a: Heart rate rises during exercise, so filling time shortens.
distractorExplanations.c: Sweat loss reduces blood volume and tends to lower stroke volume.
distractorExplanations.d: Resistance in working muscle falls during exercise; higher resistance would reduce stroke volume.

options.a: Lower blood pressure by reducing venous return
options.b: Raise intrathoracic pressure and blood pressure
options.c: Reduce spinal stability during the heavy lift
options.d: Increase oxygen delivery to the working muscles

distractorExplanations.a: Blood pressure rises during the strain; it can drop after release.
distractorExplanations.c: Breath-holding increases trunk stiffness and spinal stability.
distractorExplanations.d: Breath-holding does not improve oxygen delivery.

options.a: Raise maximal heart rate, so zones are set too low
options.b: Increase blood pressure during resistance training
options.c: Blunt the heart rate response, so zones are unreliable
options.d: Cause heart rate to spike during the warm-up only

distractorExplanations.a: Beta-blockers lower, not raise, maximal and exercise heart rate.
distractorExplanations.b: Beta-blockers usually lower blood pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: They blunt heart rate throughout exercise, not just the warm-up.

options.a: Rapid strength gains followed by a short plateau
options.b: Muscle soreness lasting 24–72 hours after training
options.c: Increased appetite during high-volume weeks
options.d: Persistent fatigue, falling performance, poor sleep

distractorExplanations.a: Gains followed by a plateau are normal training responses.
distractorExplanations.b: Short-term DOMS is normal after new or hard sessions.
distractorExplanations.c: More appetite during heavy training is expected, not a sign of overtraining.

options.a: Storing elastic energy in a quick eccentric pre-stretch
options.b: Holding a long isometric pause before the takeoff
options.c: Using a slow eccentric phase to recruit more fibers
options.d: Relying on passive ligament stretch for rebound

distractorExplanations.b: A long pause lets stored elastic energy dissipate.
distractorExplanations.c: The cycle depends on a fast eccentric phase, not a slow one.
distractorExplanations.d: The effect comes from muscle and tendon, not ligaments.

options.a: Refer to the agreement and clarify paid boundaries
options.b: Provide a few free plans to keep the relationship
options.c: Stop replying to messages without any explanation
options.d: Offer a discount only if the client posts a review

distractorExplanations.b: Ad hoc free work blurs boundaries and sets expectations.
distractorExplanations.c: Ignoring the client is unprofessional; boundaries should be stated clearly.
distractorExplanations.d: Trading discounts for reviews can be deceptive marketing.

options.a: Drink less soda and more water starting next month
options.b: Swap one 20-oz soda for water on weekdays for 4 weeks
options.c: Stop drinking soda from tomorrow and stay soda-free
options.d: Try to reduce soda intake as much as possible each week

distractorExplanations.c: An abrupt all-or-nothing quit is rarely attainable as a first step and sets no time frame for review.
distractorExplanations.d: Adding 'each week' still gives no measurable amount or end date, so progress cannot be tracked.
distractorExplanations.a: This lacks a measurable amount and a clear timeline.

options.a: Removing all flexibility from the weekly schedule
options.b: Restarting at full volume after any missed week
options.c: Planning ahead for high-risk times such as travel
options.d: Setting stricter goals after each missed session

distractorExplanations.a: Rigid schedules break easily; relapse prevention builds in flexible options.
distractorExplanations.b: Jumping back to full volume after a lapse raises soreness and dropout risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Stricter goals after a lapse increase pressure and the chance of quitting.

options.a: Drink only when thirsty, even in hot weather
options.b: Start well hydrated and replace sweat losses
options.c: Drink a liter of water just before starting
options.d: Use sports drinks instead of plain water throughout

distractorExplanations.d: Sports drinks can help in long sessions, but plain water covers most fluid needs; replacing water with them is unnecessary.
distractorExplanations.a: Thirst can lag behind fluid needs during long sessions in heat.
distractorExplanations.c: A large bolus just before exercise is poorly absorbed and uncomfortable.

options.a: Offer a moderate deficit plan with weekly check-ins
options.b: Agree only if the client's physician signs off first
options.c: Decline restrictive plans and refer to an RD or therapist
options.d: Focus on exercise and let the client manage their diet

distractorExplanations.a: Any prescribed deficit is risky with an eating disorder history and outside scope.
distractorExplanations.b: Physician sign-off does not bring clinical diet design into CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Staying silent misses a chance to refer a client with a known risk.

options.a: Is thinking about change within the next 6 months
options.b: Has been exercising regularly for over 6 months
options.c: Began exercising regularly within the last 6 months
options.d: Plans to start within 30 days and takes small steps

distractorExplanations.a: Thinking about change within six months is contemplation.
distractorExplanations.b: Six or more months of regular exercise is maintenance.
distractorExplanations.c: Recent regular exercise is the action stage.
